findings.description: exec() in the debugger interactive console (sink flagged as dynamic code execution)
findings.reasoning: This exec() is the intended core functionality of the Werkzeug interactive debugger console (an interactive Python REPL exposed over HTTP). It is not an unintended injection flaw: the console is opt-in (evalex), and the only HTTP path that reaches it is guarded in DebuggedApplication.__call__ (src/werkzeug/debug/__init__.py:514-522) which requires cmd not None, a valid frame, `self.secret == secret` (160-bit random secret not exposed to untrusted requests) and `self.check_pin_trust(environ)` (PIN/cookie based auth with failure lockout and rate limiting). The console code passed to runcode comes from `code.InteractiveInterpreter.runsource`, i.e. code typed by the authenticated operator, not from request parameters directly. CodeQL reports this as a generic "dyn-code-sink", but it is a documented, intentionally authenticated debugging feature, so it is not a vulnerability in library code.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Request args (cmd, f, s) -> DebuggedApplication.__call__ -> gated by self.secret comparison and check_pin_trust() -> execute_command -> frame.eval(command) -> _InteractiveConsole.runsource -> runcode -> exec(). Access requires both the per-process random secret and a valid PIN-authenticated trust cookie; failed attempts sleep and lock out after 10 tries.
evidence.notes: By-design debugger functionality, not attacker-reachable without the debugger secret + PIN. Considered FP for the library.

The variable names inserted into the AST come from route parameter converter names inside the developer-authored rule string (`<converter:name>`), and `_convert()`/`_prefix_names()` build a call node using `ast.Name(str(elem))` — an identifier node validated by `ast.parse` of the template, not raw text interpolation into an executed string. Route rules are part of application source code (Map/Rule definitions), not derived from user input, so an attacker cannot control what is compiled. This is a legitimate code-generation optimization for URL building, not an injection sink.

findings.description: Multipart form parser (Werkzeug 2.2.2) has no limit on the number of multipart parts (no max_form_parts), allowing an unauthenticated attacker to exhaust server memory/disk and CPU (CVE-2023-25577)
findings.code_snippet:
class MultiPartParser:
    def __init__(
        self,
        stream_factory: t.Optional["TStreamFactory"] = None,
        charset: str = "utf-8",
        errors: str = "replace",
        max_form_memory_size: t.Optional[int] = None,
        cls: t.Optional[t.Type[MultiDict]] = None,
        buffer_size: int = 64 * 1024,
    ) -> None:
        self.charset = charset
        self.errors = errors
        self.max_form_memory_size = max_form_memory_size
findings.reasoning: Confirmed Werkzeug version is 2.2.2 (src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6 -> __version__ = "2.2.2"), i.e. before the CVE-2023-25577 fix in 2.2.3/2.3.0 which added `max_form_parts` and a hard cap on parts. In this tree the only guards are `max_content_length` (checked in FormDataParser.parse, formparser.py:246-254) and `max_form_memory_size` (formparser.py:282-289, 302-311; sansio/multipart.py:131-138). Neither bounds the *number* of parts. MultiPartParser.parse() (formparser.py ~line 361-430) loops over every part produced by MultipartDecoder and appends each `Field`/`File` into the `fields`/`files` lists with no counter and no limit; for each `File` part it also calls `start_file_streaming()` which allocates a new SpooledTemporaryFile/TemporaryFile (formparser.py:38-48). An attacker can therefore send a single request with `Content-Type: multipart/form-data` containing tens of thousands of tiny parts. content_length stays small (so max_content_length does not trigger) and the buffered part data is flushed per-part (so max_form_memory_size never accumulates), yet the parser creates one MultiDict entry and one tempfile/spooled buffer per part -> unbounded memory and file-descriptor/temp-file consumption -> OOM / fd exhaustion / DoS. This is exactly the vulnerability fixed upstream by `max_form_parts` (default 1000) plus the RequestEntityTooLarge raise on exceeding it. There is no mitigation anywhere in this codebase (grep for `max_form_parts` returns 0 matches).

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Remote request body -> WSGI environ ('wsgi.input', CONTENT_TYPE, CONTENT_LENGTH) -> Request.form/multipart entrypoint -> FormDataParser.parse_from_environ (formparser.py:255-264) -> FormDataParser.parse (formparser.py:266-290) -> _parse_multipart (formparser.py:292-310) -> MultiPartParser.parse (formparser.py:361-430) -> unbounded loop creating one MultiDict entry + one temp file per part. Only length-based limits exist; part-count is unbounded.
evidence.notes: CVE-2023-25577 / GHSA-f7xr-j4x7-9x6q. Fixed upstream in Werkzeug 2.2.3 and 2.3.0 by adding `max_form_parts` (default 1000). The same missing limit is reflected by the related query results at wrappers/request.py:84 (max_form_memory_size exists, max_form_parts absent) and formparser.py:128-201.

findings.description: sansio/multipart.py MultipartDecoder.receive_data/next_event lack part-count and dropped-bytes accounting (no num_bytes_dropped), enabling CPU/quadratic and memory exhaustion DoS (CVE-2023-46136 family)
findings.reasoning: MultipartDecoder is the low-level event decoder used by MultiPartParser (formparser.py:382). Its only resource guard is the single `max_form_memory_size` check on the buffered (in-memory) bytearray; there is no accounting of how much data has been discarded/skipped, no cap on the number of boundary/part transitions, and no cap on the number of `Preamble`/`Field`/`File` events it emits. `next_event()` re-runs `self.preamble_re.search(...)`/`self.boundary_re.search(...)` from `_search_position` on every call, and `last_newline()` performs `rindex` on the whole buffer; an attacker can craft a body with a very long or adversarial preamble/epilogue without any boundary match, so the regex scan is repeated over the growing buffer repeatedly (quadratic CPU). Combined with an unbounded number of boundary markers (a couple of bytes each), a small request creates a huge number of decode events and Python-object churn. Upstream fixed this class of issue by tracking discarded bytes (`num_bytes_dropped`) and limiting total parts; neither exists here (grep for 'num_bytes_dropped' -> 0 matches). Result: remote unauthenticated CPU/memory exhaustion.

evidence.code_context: src/werkzeug/sansio/multipart.py:131-138 receive_data (shown). next_event() at lines 141-180 repeatedly calls self.preamble_re.search(self.buffer, self._search_position) and re-computes self._search_position = max(0, len(self.buffer) - len(self.boundary) - SEARCH_EXTRA_LENGTH). last_newline() (lines 118-131) does self.buffer.rindex(b'\n')/rindex(b'\r') over the whole buffer. Grep for 'num_bytes_dropped' -> 0 matches; grep for 'max_form_parts' -> 0 matches.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Attacker-controlled request body (wsgi.input) -> _make_chunk_iter -> MultiPartParser.parse (formparser.py:382-386) -> MultipartDecoder.receive_data(data) -> self.buffer.extend(data) -> MultipartDecoder.next_event() repeated regex searches over the growing buffer with no discarded-byte accounting or part cap.
evidence.notes: Related to CVE-2023-46136 (excessive resource consumption in the multipart parser, fixed in 2.3.8/3.0.1) and shares root cause with CVE-2023-25577 (unbounded parts). Version confirmed 2.2.2 at src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6.

findings.description: CodeQL flags the containment checks inside safe_join itself (normpath, alt-sep check, isabs, '..' prefix check, posixpath.join) as unsafe path handling, but these lines ARE the sanitizer/enforcement logic, not a traversable sink
findings.reasoning:
The 6 CodeQL results (lines 128, 131, 132, 134, 138, 140) all point at the body of `werkzeug.security.safe_join`, whose entire purpose is to *prevent* path traversal. Each flagged "attribute/any call" is part of the defense:

- L128 `posixpath.normpath(filename)` canonicalizes `..`/`.` segments and duplicate slashes before any check, so "a/../../b" becomes "../b" and is then rejected.
- L131 `any(sep in filename for sep in _os_alt_seps)`: `_os_alt_seps` is built at module import (L14-16) as `[s for s in (os.path.sep, os.path.altsep) if s and s != "/"]`, i.e. it contains exactly the non-"/" separators for the current OS (e.g. "\\" on Windows). Any such separator in an untrusted component causes `None`.
- L132 `os.path.isabs(filename)` rejects absolute paths (including "//host/share" and "C:\\..." on the platforms where they are absolute).
- L134 `filename.startswith("../")` (plus `filename == ".."` at L133) rejects any parent-directory escape that survives normpath.
- L140 `posixpath.join(*parts)` only runs when all components passed the checks, and posixpath.join cannot reintroduce a traversal because ".."/leading-slash/alt-separator components were already rejected.

Because the loop rejects (returns None) on every escaping component instead of propagating it, there is no tainted path reaching a filesystem sink. All consumers correctly handle the None return: `utils.send_from_directory` (L574-577 raises NotFound), `middleware/shared_data.py` L168-171 and L204-207 return `(None, None)`. No bypass was found: the version-specific edge cases (empty trusted dir -> "./" prefix per tests/test_security.py::test_safe_join_empty_trusted, Windows drive-relative "c:test.txt" remaining inside the directory) do not escape the base directory. These results are the classic "sanitizer internals" pattern emitted by py/safe-join-internals and are false positives.

evidence.code_context:
L14-18: _os_alt_seps = list(sep for sep in [os.path.sep, os.path.altsep] if sep is not None and sep != "/")

L110-140 safe_join: normalizes each component, then bails out (return None) on alt-sep presence, absolute path, ".." or "../" prefix; only then posixpath.join(*parts).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: No taint flow: untrusted components are terminated at the checks (return None) rather than appended. Callers os.fspath() the inputs (utils.send_from_directory L574) and treat None as NotFound / no-opener (shared_data.py L168-171, L204-207), so no attacker-controlled string reaches open().
evidence.notes: tests/test_security.py L32-49 assert safe_join("foo", "../bar/baz") is None, alt-sep injection is None, and empty-trusted-dir yields './c:test.txt' (still inside). Also confirmed safe_join is only imported by utils.py and middleware/shared_data.py, both of which handle None.

findings.description: safe_join's containment checks (normpath + alt-sep/isabs/'..' checks) correctly block POSIX path traversal; flagged calls are the intended sanitizer logic, not a vulnerability
findings.reasoning: The CodeQL rule `py/safe-join-internals` reports the internal calls made inside `safe_join` (posixpath.normpath, `sep in filename`, os.path.isabs, filename.startswith) as an audit hook so a reviewer can verify the containment logic. On inspection the logic is the hardened implementation: every untrusted component is first canonicalised with `posixpath.normpath` (collapsing `a/../../b` and `./` sequences), then rejected if it contains the platform alternate separator (`\` on Windows, from `_os_alt_seps`), is an absolute path (`os.path.isabs`), is exactly `..`, or starts with `../`. After normalisation a component can only escape by starting with `../` or being absolute, and both are rejected, so the base directory cannot be escaped on POSIX. Verified against the shipped test suite (tests/test_security.py:32-49) which asserts `safe_join("foo", "../bar/baz") is None` and `safe_join("foo", "foo\\bar") is None` on Windows. These reported lines therefore represent the mitigation, not a vulnerability (the query fires on any call inside a function named safe_join, regardless of correctness).

evidence.code_context: _os_alt_seps = [sep for sep in [os.path.sep, os.path.altsep] if sep is not None and sep != "/"]
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Untrusted `path` from send_from_directory (src/werkzeug/utils.py:574) / SharedDataMiddleware loaders (src/werkzeug/middleware/shared_data.py:168,204) reaches safe_join; each component is normpath'ed and rejected on alt-sep, isabs, '..' or '../' prefix before posixpath.join, so no traversal is possible on POSIX.
evidence.notes: Query is informational (audit of safe_join internals); reported calls are the sanitizer itself. Tests confirm behaviour.

findings.description: posixpath.join at the end of safe_join joins only validated components; no traversal reachable from Werkzeug callers in this version
findings.code_snippet: return posixpath.join(*parts)
findings.reasoning: The join is performed with `posixpath.join` over `parts` whose first element is the trusted base directory (defaulted to "." when empty, precisely so the first untrusted component cannot become the root) and whose remaining elements have each already passed the normpath/alt-sep/isabs/'../' checks above. Because `posixpath.join` does not reset to an absolute path unless a component is absolute, and absolute components are rejected, the result stays under the base directory. All in-tree consumers are upstream of this guarantee: `send_from_directory` (utils.py:574) raises NotFound() when None is returned and SharedDataMiddleware loaders (shared_data.py:168/204) return (None, None) before opening the file. Residual Windows-specific concern (drive-relative components such as `D:foo`, or UNC/device paths, where `os.path.isabs` is host-dependent) is the known CVE-2024-49766 class of issue that was hardened in later releases by additionally comparing the drive/root of the joined result, but no demonstrable escape exists in this code for the components that survive the checks (backslash alt-seps are rejected, `xx/../../y` is collapsed to `../y` and rejected), so this reported join call is not a confirmed exploitable vulnerability.

evidence.code_context: parts = [directory]; ... parts.append(filename) ; return posixpath.join(*parts)
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Sources: WSGI path from send_from_directory / SharedDataMiddleware loader. Sink: open()/reader.open_resource(). Every component is normpath'ed and filtered before the join; `safe_join` returns None on any suspicious component and callers abort.
evidence.notes: Only theoretical Windows drive-relative edge case remains; not demonstrably exploitable with the checks present in 2.2.2.

findings.description: CodeQL flagged the internal `any(sep in filename ...)` containment check inside werkzeug's safe_join; this is the sanitizer itself, not a vulnerability
findings.reasoning: safe_join normalizes each untrusted component with posixpath.normpath() and then rejects the component if it contains any OS alternate separator (line 131), is absolute (os.path.isabs), is exactly "..", or starts with "../". Only after passing all these checks is the component joined onto the trusted base directory with posixpath.join. Therefore line 131 is part of the traversal *defense*, not a sink: there is no path construction using unvalidated input here. CodeQL's py/safe-join-internals query reports the internal helper calls within the recommended API itself (a "containment audit"), which produces uniform false positives when the code under review is the canonical safe implementation. No caller-controllable path escapes the base directory through this statement.

evidence.notes: Line 131 is a guard (any(sep in filename for sep in _os_alt_seps)); returning None prevents traversal. _os_alt_seps excludes '/' and only holds backslash-like separators for cross-platform hardening.

findings.description: CodeQL flagged os.path.isabs() inside safe_join's validation of untrusted path components; this is the traversal mitigation, not a vulnerable sink

It performs no filesystem access and builds no path from the input. The result of this call is only used as a negative condition in the rejection branch; the final path is produced by posixpath.join(directory, validated_components) after all checks pass. Hence there is no path traversal here — this line is precisely the containment enforcement CodeQL's safe-join-internals audit is meant to verify exists.

Because normalization collapses interior `a/../../b` forms into a leading "../" (which is then rejected), the check is effective. findings.description: CodeQL flagged posixpath.join in safe_join; the join only receives the trusted directory plus components that already passed traversal validation
findings.code_snippet: return posixpath.join(*parts)
findings.reasoning: This is the only place a path is constructed, and every element of `parts` after index 0 has already been rejected if it was absolute, contained an alternate separator, was "..", or started with "../". Also, when `directory` is empty it is replaced with "." so the first untrusted component cannot be treated as the trusted base (documented and covered by tests/test_security.py::test_safe_join_empty_trusted). posixpath.join is used for consistent POSIX semantics regardless of host OS. An empty-string component is appended as-is but cannot escape the base. No caller in the codebase (middleware/shared_data.py, utils.send_from_directory) can bypass these guards; both treat a None return as 404/not-found. Therefore the reported call is the sanctioned construction step of a correctly hardened helper — false positive.

evidence.callers: src/werkzeug/middleware/shared_data.py:168 (get_package_loader), :204 (get_directory_loader), src/werkzeug/utils.py:574 (send_from_directory) — all return 404/None when safe_join yields None
evidence.tests: tests/test_security.py:32-49 cover 'foo/../bar', 'foo\\bar' on nt, injected alt sep '*', and directory='' with 'c:test.txt'

findings.description: Werkzeug 2.2.2 parse_cookie silently drops nameless cookies (CVE-2023-23934), allowing __Host-/__Secure- cookie prefix confusion
findings.reasoning: This is the upstream-affected code of Werkzeug 2.2.2 (see src/werkzeug/__init__.py: __version__ = "2.2.2"). The low-level parser (_cookie_parse_impl, _internal.py:381) uses the regex `(?P<key>[^=;]+)(?:\s*=\s*(?P<val>...))?\s*;` where the `=` and the value are OPTIONAL. Consequences: (1) A nameless cookie such as `Cookie: =__Host-foo=bar` — the regex cannot match an empty key at position 0 (the `[^=;]+` cannot match `=`), so `re.search` skips ahead and the *next* token is consumed as the key; the nameless cookie is silently discarded instead of being reported/rejected. (2) Because a key is only stripped and later `if not key_str: continue`, an empty name is never surfaced to callers. Browsers normally refuse to send nameless cookies, but an attacker who controls a value that ends up in the Cookie header (e.g. via a client-side `document.cookie` injection, an intermediary, a sub-domain, or any component that concatenates cookie strings) can create a situation where the application and the browser disagree about cookie names. This is exactly the CVE-2023-23934 defect: the fix in 2.2.3 changed the cookie regex/parsing so the `=` is required and empty/nameless cookie names are no longer silently accepted, so `__Host-`/`__Secure-` prefixed names cannot be spoofed or confused. Applications relying on `__Host-` prefixes (cookie fixation / overwrite protections) can therefore be bypassed because parse_cookie reports the attacker-controlled cookie under the privileged name.

evidence.code_context: src/werkzeug/sansio/http.py:97 parse_cookie -> _parse_pairs -> _cookie_parse_impl(cookie) (src/werkzeug/_internal.py:381-394). Regex at src/werkzeug/_internal.py:35-46: rb'''(?P<key>[^=;]+)(?:\s*=\s*(?P<val>"(?:[^\\"]|\\.)*" | (?:.*?)))?\s*;''' with re.VERBOSE -- the '=' group is OPTIONAL, so 'foo;' parses as key 'foo' with empty value and a leading '=' is skipped by re.search.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: HTTP_COOKIE header -> http.parse_cookie(header) (src/werkzeug/http.py:1117-1148, extracts header['HTTP_COOKIE']) -> _sansio_http.parse_cookie(cookie=...) -> _cookie_parse_impl(cookie) -> MultiDict returned to application code that checks cookie prefixes (e.g. __Host-session).
evidence.notes: Repository version is 2.2.2 (src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6), the last version vulnerable to CVE-2023-23934 (GHSA-pq67-2wwv-3xjx). No length/prefix/empty-name validation exists anywhere in the parse chain. Upstream fix (2.2.3) required '=' in the regex and rejected nameless cookies.

findings.description: Cookie regex in _cookie_parse_impl makes '=' optional and cannot match an empty key, so nameless cookies are skipped/merged (root cause of CVE-2023-23934)
findings.code_snippet:
def _cookie_parse_impl(b: bytes) -> t.Iterator[t.Tuple[bytes, bytes]]:
    """Lowlevel cookie parsing facility that operates on bytes."""
    i = 0
    n = len(b)

    while i < n:
        match = _cookie_re.search(b + b";", i)
        if not match:
            break

        key = match.group("key").strip()
        value = match.group("val") or b""
        i = match.end(0)

        yield key, _cookie_unquote(value)
findings.reasoning:
Root cause location. `_cookie_re` (lines 35-46) is:
  (?P<key>[^=;]+)(?:\s*=\s*(?P<val>"(?:[^\\"]|\\.)*" | (?:.*?)))?\s*;
Two defects, both fixed upstream in 2.2.3 for CVE-2023-23934:
1. The `= value` part is OPTIONAL, so a token without `=` (e.g. `foo;`) is accepted as a cookie with an empty value instead of being rejected.
2. `[^=;]+` requires at least one non-`=` character, so an empty name (a cookie starting with `=`, e.g. `=bar;`) cannot be matched at the current offset. `re.search` then silently advances and matches a *later* segment, so the nameless cookie is dropped entirely and the next cookie (possibly carrying the `__Host-`/`__Secure-` prefix, with leading whitespace stripped by `.strip()`) is reported as if legitimately sent by the browser.
Since `_cookie_parse_impl` is the single low-level parser used by `sansio.http.parse_cookie` (line 127) and hence by `werkzeug.http.parse_cookie` used by all request wrappers, every Werkzeug application inherits the cookie-name confusion. This is a true positive for CWE-20 (improper input validation) / CWE-345 (insufficient verification of data authenticity).

evidence.code_context: src/werkzeug/_internal.py:35-46 _cookie_re = re.compile(rb'''(?P<key>[^=;]+)(?:\s*=\s*(?P<val>"(?:[^\\"]|\\.)*" | (?:.*?)))?\s*;''', flags=re.VERBOSE); parser loop at 381-394 uses re.search(b + b';', i) and match.group('key').strip().
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Cookie header bytes -> _cookie_re.search -> key = match.group('key').strip() -> yielded to sansio.http._parse_pairs -> ds.MultiDict consumed by app code relying on __Host-/__Secure- names.
evidence.notes: Upstream 2.2.3 fix changed this regex so '=' is mandatory and an empty key can be matched/detected; 2.2.2 (this repo, src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6) is vulnerable. Behavior verification: parse_cookie('=a; __Host-x=y') -> {'__Host-x': 'y'}, the nameless cookie is discarded instead of rejected.

findings.reasoning: The py/host-prefix-literal query flags the literal "Host" in `X-Forwarded-Host`. This is an HTTP proxy header name in a docstring, not a `__Host-` cookie prefix, and no cookie parsing logic is involved. The same applies to the two other results of this query (src/werkzeug/sansio/utils.py:62-81 and src/werkzeug/wsgi.py:96-112), which are `get_host()` docstrings that merely mention the ``Host`` header. There is no trust-boundary bypass in these docstring locations; ProxyFix itself legitimately documents which headers it trusts and requires the operator to configure the trusted proxy count (x_host=N). No code pattern here allows bypassing `__Host-` prefix enforcement.

findings.description: Public legacy wrapper `werkzeug.http.parse_cookie` propagates the nameless-cookie parsing flaw (CVE-2023-23934) to all WSGI-app callers
findings.reasoning: This is the primary public entry point applications call (or that Request.cookies routes through) for parsing the attacker-controlled `HTTP_COOKIE` header. It performs no validation of its own and delegates straight to `sansio.http.parse_cookie`, which in Werkzeug 2.2.2 (see `src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6`) uses `_cookie_parse_impl` whose regex makes `=value` optional and silently drops empty keys. Consequently a malformed/nameless cookie in `Cookie: =a; __Host-session=evil` is discarded without raising, and the resulting MultiDict still exposes a `__Host-…`-shaped name that the attacker supplied — the exact invariant bypass of CVE-2023-23934. Because this wrapper is the API exposed to user code, it widens the affected surface beyond sansio callers.

evidence.code_context: http.py:1117 parse_cookie -> _sansio_http.parse_cookie(cookie=cookie, charset=..., errors=..., cls=...) with no validation of cookie names or '=' presence.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: HTTP_COOKIE (WSGI environ, attacker controlled) -> header['HTTP_COOKIE'] -> sansio.http.parse_cookie -> _cookie_parse_impl -> MultiDict; no sanitization at any hop.
evidence.notes: Werkzeug 2.2.2 confirmed by grep of src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6 (__version__ = '2.2.2'); fix for CVE-2023-23934 landed in 2.2.3 requiring '=' in the cookie regex.

findings.description: Werkzeug debugger console authentication (pin_auth / check_pin_trust) does not validate the request Host header, so the interactive debugger is reachable from any host (DNS rebinding / non-local access), leading to RCE (CVE-2024-34069).
findings.code_snippet:
def pin_auth(self, request: Request) -> Response:
        """Authenticates with the pin."""
        exhausted = False
        auth = False
        trust = self.check_pin_trust(request.environ)
        pin = t.cast(str, self.pin)

        # If the trust return value is `None` it means that the cookie is
        # set but the stored pin hash value is bad.  This means that the
        # pin was changed.  In this case we count a bad auth and unset the
        # cookie.  This way it becomes harder to guess the cookie name
        # instead of the pin as we still count up failures.
        bad_cookie = False
        if trust is None:
            self._fail_pin_auth()
            bad_cookie = True

        # If we're trusted, we're authenticated.
        elif trust:
            auth = True

        # If we failed too many times, then we're locked out.
        elif self._failed_pin_auth > 10:
            exhausted = True

        # Otherwise go through pin based authentication
        else:
            entered_pin = request.args["pin"]

            if entered_pin.strip().replace("-", "") == pin.replace("-", ""):
                self._failed_pin_auth = 0
                auth = True
            else:
                self._fail_pin_auth()

        rv = Response(
            json.dumps({"auth": auth, "exhausted": exhausted}),
            mimetype="application/json",
        )
        if auth:
            rv.set_cookie(
                self.pin_cookie_name,
                f"{int(time.time())}|{hash_pin(pin)}",
                httponly=True,
                samesite="Strict",
                secure=request.is_secure,
            )
        elif bad_cookie:
            rv.delete_cookie(self.pin_cookie_name)
        return rv
findings.reasoning: In this version (2.2.2) the debugger's authentication logic contains no Host-header validation whatsoever. `pin_auth()` (line 439) and `check_pin_trust()` (line 413) only look at the `__werkzeug_debugger_*` pin cookie hash/timestamp — neither compares `request.host`/`environ['HTTP_HOST']` against a set of trusted hosts (grep for `trusted_hosts`/`host_is_trusted` in the debugger package returns nothing; the helpers exist only in `sansio/utils.py` and `wsgi.py` and are never used by the debugger). Consequently, when a developer runs the dev server with `debug=True` and a non-localhost bind (`host="0.0.0.0"`), any remote party can reach `/console` and the `__debugger__=yes` endpoints; a malicious web page can additionally use DNS rebinding to make the victim's browser talk to `127.0.0.1:<port>` while the debugger still sees the attacker's domain as Host, defeating the implicit localhost-only assumption. Once the pin is obtained/brute-forced (the failure counter is per-process, reset by restart, and the response distinguishes auth/exhausted), the resulting pin cookie makes `check_pin_trust()` return True, and the dispatch code at line 529 (`self.execute_command(request, cmd, frame)`) evaluates the attacker-supplied `cmd` inside the console frame — arbitrary code execution. The upstream fix (3.0.3) added a `trusted_hosts` parameter and a `host_is_trusted(get_host(environ), self.trusted_hosts)` check inside `check_pin_trust`, exactly the check that is missing here.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: attacker-controlled HTTP request (Host header + `__debugger__`/`cmd`/`f`/`frm`/`s` query params) -> DebuggedApplication.__call__ -> pin_auth()/check_pin_trust() (no Host validation) -> execute_command() -> eval of `cmd` inside _ConsoleFrame namespace. Nothing between the untrusted Host header / request and the console restricts origin of the caller.
evidence.notes: grep for 'trusted_hosts' and 'host_is_trusted' shows these exist only in src/werkzeug/sansio/utils.py, src/werkzeug/sansio/request.py and src/werkzeug/wsgi.py; the debug package (src/werkzeug/debug/) never imports or uses them -> the CVE-2024-34069 host-trust check is absent. Version confirmed 2.2.2 in src/werkzeug/__init__.py:6 (fix landed in 3.0.3).
